title: Discussion about the Importance of Film Movements

commenti.body:
I'm intrigued by your blog and will definitely look at it in the coming days, bookmarked already.

For me what's interesting at first glance is what gets to be called a movement and what doesn't. This seems to depend on the whim of a critic or group of influential critics at particular moments when it comes to naming these putative movements. Though there may well be validity in grouping films or filmmakers in this way, it's strange what doesn't get a label. 

Just to give one example, it's clear that in the 1990s there was a wave of Anglo-American noirish films with a sharp sense of irony and verbal wit, of which Tarantino was the best-known exponent and Scorsese's ***Goodfellas*** perhaps the foundation. But unlike noir films of the classic age, they favoured sharp camera moves, flashy editing and attention-grabbing soundtracks with memorable needle drops. This "movement" never got an official name but was very clearly a thing. Then the moment passed and the time to give it a name also. Nowadays people say "Tarantinoesque" or something like that to describe ***Things to do in Denver When You're Dead*** or ***Snatch***, but that perhaps puts a lot of weight on one individual. 

There are in my mind many other weird exceptions to the "movement" rules. Italian neorealism was supposed to have died out in the 1960s, so what do you call Novecento or The Tree of Wooden Clogs? Neo-neorealism?

I'm intrigued by your ideas and will for sure follow them closely...

I am glad you find it useful! Goal was to create a portal dedicated for film movements given that there is non on the web.   


Yes, definitely it is an interesting topic deciphering what gets to be called a movement and what dont, as I concentrated in representing the "famous ones" which are, at this moment, non debatable. For example, the most recent one being Greek Weird Wave, which is still in the making by critics.   


How did you research film movements? Were you actively watching and reading about them or was it a more passive approach?

Very interesting website, going to definitely deep dive into  it later. I'd love to hear your thoughts on a pet theory of mine regarding film movements, and overall trends. The idea is that their might be an overall movement, let's say American New Wave. Which is typically defined as from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s, but within that there are five year micro movements or periods that are more easily definable. 

Think of 1965 - 1969 as the proto American New Wave where things were getting pushed further into taboo subjects but weren't necessarily as formally innovative or coming from young directors. Then you get the real meat and potatoes of the New Hollywood wave of directors coming in from 1970 - 1975, and finally their development as artists after 1975.  
In general this could be done to every film movements, wave, or period, as there's going to be a wide difference between the beginning and end of a movement.

You picked a great example for the theory. Some others would be Parallel Cinema, Iranian New Wave and New Mexican Cinema. I agree that there are periods within the movements but I wouldnt call them micro movements as they are still closely related.   


In the blog, I didnt delve that much into it, because it would have take a lot of time. But there are clearly different periods in some cases, and New Hollywood is a prime example of that. I actually researched it divided in periods because of the sheer difference, and its easier exploring that way - given that the movement is massive.

I think waves and movements are terms most commonly used by film historians and film scholars in trying to make sense of a specific time and what can connect the movies in question. These are groups that your standard cinephile rarely gets in contact with and thus the usage and creation of these terms can seem confusing perhaps? Of course there are certain movements that are based on other things, such as the Dogme 95 movement. 
But yes, I think its mostly useable in an academic and mostly film historian context. Of course films after can have similar traits, such as the neo-realism youre talking about, but using that term for films outside of the time period of neo-realism is not useful for historians. Also, for neo-realism there is an argument for keeping it contained within a time-frame, as much of it was a reaction to the horrors of the war and all that came with it.

I would agree with this.

Of course, thinking about movements makes it easier to think about film history, but, just like with art movements or literary movements, it's important to remember that it's essential an abstraction, a label given in hindsight. Wordsworth and Coleridge did not call themselves Romantic poets; Picasso and Braque did not call themselves cubists.

Definitely just a casual thing, I have very little interest in the "meta" side of critical theory, but since these sub-generic labels can be a useful way of thinking about film, I do pay some attention to them and use them in my essays/reviews. 

Having thought about it a little, I have a suggestion for your site: maybe to have a section where you propose or investigate new movements, by which I mean revealing existing tendencies. 

BTW I've never heard of Greek Weird Wave before now, apart from Lanthimos I would have no idea of who would go in that.

Here's a passing thought: Julia Ducournau and Bertrand Bonello, are they part of a movement? I've heard some put them into New French Extremity, but that seems reductive to me. Maybe there's another thing which would include young Gavras, I'd suggest [Enragés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrag%C3%A9s) like in the French Revolution.

Yes, I agree with that. There are however some that come from a common idea formed by the creators themselves, such as the manifestos of the Dogme movement and the neorealist movement (although Zavattinis manifesto was not as important as the Dogme one).   


While those that want to learn more about film do not necessarily have to become film scholars, I would suggest to OP to read some introductionary film scholar literature if they are to delve into some more theoretical terms, such as any introductionary book by Bordwell or Corrigan & White.

Bordwell is excellent. OP, would particularly recommend *On the History of Film Style,* for a more scholarly read, or *Film Art* for an introduction.

Also VF Perkins' *Film as Film.*

Oh I definitely believe in diving into a genre. There’s so much to be gained by diving into blaxploitation. Gaining that knowledge of the time. Taking in the genre. Blacula, Black Mama White Mama, Friday Foster, Foxy Brown, Coffy, Shaft. It’s such a great genre, but the experience you create for yourself during can be magical. Immerse yourself in drive-in culture of the 70’s. Drive-ins back then had hamburgers, hot dogs, onion rings, in addition to popcorn. People would bring malt liquor and smoke a blunt or a cigar. You can make that stuff at home for a party, or just order in. Then put on Super Fly. It feels like you’re back in the day. And it’s so interesting to watch the acting and think about how much acting has changed over the years.

The problem with these cinematic movements is that they are to the history of cinema what braces and acne outbreaks are to adolescence: the highly visible, very local and temporary eruptive phase of a much broader and deeper process. To focus on these movements is to miss the great periods in the history of cinema... A bit like focusing on the French Revolution or Columbus's arrival in America, without ever considering the huge periods of "Antiquity", "Middle Ages" or "Renaissance", which are far more important for conceptualizing and understanding world history.

Of course, Italian neo-realism and German expressionism were fundamental turning points in the history of cinema. But it's more telling to understand what each was part of, what they were a symptom of. To understand that Italian neoralism, along with Orson Welles the same years (the early forties), was the very first manifestation of modern cinema, of a new relationship with the spectator, which would mature, transform cinema in a muted way, then explode visibly 15 years later with the new waves. Or to understand that German Expressionism was just one of the many avant-garde movements of the 1920s (trans-artistic, trans-national, and theorized movements seeking alternatives to classical mise-en-scène)...

So overall, beyond studying these currents, I think it's more important to understand the major aesthetic phases (primitive cinema, classical cinema, modern cinema...).

Cool topic. I went to school for film and we learned about movements, indie films,  international films, etc… I definitely prefer Italian New Wave over French New Wave.

I feel like most countries have their own “new wave.” Polish New Wave is pretty cool, I also like Hong Kong, Taiwanese, Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese New Wave. New Indian Cinema is also great

There are some great Indian auteurs like Satyajit Ray

I started watching Goddard and loved Alphaville so much and I thought a bit about the idea that some people have that some of these French New Wave movies are made to be complex and "genre breaking" or whatever. I thought surely they must not have gone out with the thought to make super complex films that were confusing. Then I decided to watch Pierrot Le Fou (Pierrot the Fool) next by Goddard, lmao. I could not have been more wrong, I've never seen a film that more exemplifies the idea of trying to be complex and meta-fictional and break filmic norms. But as a surrealist literature junkie I loved it even more.

So at least with French New-Wave I found it to be very important.

Your blog is really interesting! I've always liked to binge watch films from the same aesthetic movement. Especially when a theatre or cinematheque dedicates a whole program/retrospective. This way I've discovered the overlooked films of the Japanese New Wave, Prague Spring, Iranian New Wave, Lettrism, Soviet Montage...  
I also tried to [map out the history of film movements](https://screenville.blogspot.com/2012/09/nuances-in-art-cinema-history.html) with their main auteurs, by comparing the parallel evolution of the Mainstream, Budget, Art Cinema and Experimental...

One of the favorite films and definitely the favorite director, love Cassavetes! He was a predecessors and one of the influences to the New Hollywood, but he was mostly an outsider, thats why Shadows is a pioneering work of Independent film. 

Later, in the 1970s, he was more acquainted with the New Hollywood movement, still I would categorize him and his "Faces Distribution" as a part of Independent film.

I recommend, if you havnt seen it yet, to check his work "Too Late Blues". He did it under studio system, yes, but you can definitely see his independent and creative spirit, its truly a must watch for any Cassavetes fan.

Thank you both for recommendations, with some I'm familiar, but will have to check the others out. The goal of the website was more of a surface level introduction, an accessible 5 minutes read to point out the origins, characteristics, major filmmakers and films, as well as the influence and legacy. Just to spark an interest and make it more accessible to delve into the matter - a stepping stone. 

Of course, I am certainly not a film scholar, and I am simply not able to provide a more in dept content, but as I pointed out, that wasn't the goal. Something that can be added to the site is what to read next, for people wanting to continue exploring and study deeper.

Same, Italian Neorealism suit me more. Actually, I am still not able to enjoy French New Wave after like 10+ years, its just not for me. I see the importance, and they can be definitely a worthy watch, entertaining wise as well as intellectually, but I just cant seem to enjoy them fully. 

Taiwanese and Hong Kong New Waves are in my favorites tho. Czechoslovak too.

Woooooow, this is amazing! I am a crazy about those charts/mappings of the periods, genres etc. Once I created the same for music genres, how they interconnected, influences each others, more in a style of "family three", but this, wow. Ill download it to have on my PC. 

Will also PM you about certain questions :)

Thank you, you're most welcome. I'm guessing you wonder about the color coding...

Please add "Contemplative Cinema" too to your already great blog!
One underrated, extremely entertaining blaxploitation film I'd highly recommend is *Truck Turner* (1974), starring the late Isaac Hayes.
Iranian and Czech new waves as well.
You're very welcome.
Yeah those are also great
Same, I agree. The only two French New Wave films I cared for were Hiroshima Mon Amour and Vagabond. They’re very different than most of the French New Wave films
